title: Chart Builder
context: Grade 5, the pages on metric measures. An adult sees a place value chart with unit names on it. What the pages are doing is making every unit a neighbour of every other: each is 10 times the unit to its right, and a measure written one digit to a unit is already a decimal, once its unit is named.

writeup.why: Name the standard units, read the prefixes against the base unit, see that each unit is 10 times the unit to its right, and read a measure written one digit to a unit as one decimal with its unit.
writeup.look: A chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, three standard unit cards above it, and digit tiles that drop into the columns.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Chart Builder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of units placed on the chart. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The chart fills the lower part of the area: seven columns, each 140 wide, from x 90 to x 1070, headed kilo, hecto, deca, the base unit, deci, centi and milli from left to right, with three rows at y 430, y 520 and y 610 for length, weight and capacity. The unit names in the cells are violet, labelled Unit, and the base unit column in the middle, metre, gram and litre, has a heavier ink outline. Above the chart, along y 240, stand the three standard unit cards, metre, kilogram and litre, each 200 by 110, with the tray of things beside them at x 820, y 240 on the first phase. On the second phase the six prefix cards lie face down over their column heads, and a turned card shows its worth against the base unit as a violet Unit fact on a strip at y 360. On the third phase the amber marker sits over one column, the Step left button stands at x 900, y 250, and ten small bars of the unit to the right slide together into one bar of the new unit along y 330, the step drawn as a vermilion arrow labelled Move. On the fourth phase the deep blue digit tiles, labelled Given, wait in a tray at x 120, y 250, drop one to a column, and the point snaps into the gap just after the column it is dropped on; a grey zero, labelled Place holder, fills a column left open. The decimal read back sits in green, labelled Answer, at x 120, y 690, with its unit name. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a delete key, and one key for each unit name of the row in use. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. The measure the question gives, in the unit it is given in, is deep blue, labelled Given or Measure. The measure the working reaches, and a reading on a scale, is green, labelled Answer, Reading or Same measure. The places moved across the unit chart, and the worth of one small mark on a scale, are vermilion, labelled Move or One mark. A unit fact, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet, labelled Unit fact, Unit or Other scale. The part taken away, and a part left over after sharing, are rose, labelled Taken away or Left over. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open inside a number, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. Rulers, tapes, jugs, scales, thermometer tubes, chart lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The chart stays built, with the last measure's digits in their columns, the point after its unit and the decimal read beside it in green.

phases.win: every thing sits on its standard unit, and the three cards light together
phases.does: drags each thing onto the standard unit that measures it
phases.goal: the metre measures length, the kilogram measures weight and the litre measures capacity; these are the standard units
phases.says: What would you measure this with? Drop it on its unit.
phases.check: Away from the screen: name one thing at home you would measure in litres, and one in kilograms.
phases.feels: the three cards lighting together once every thing is home
phases.hands: Put three paper cards on a desk saying metre, kilogram and litre. Pick up a ribbon, a bag of rice and a bottle of water, and put each on the card that measures it.
phases.tries: First rung: sort just two things, one to measure along and one to lift. Second rung: add one thing to pour. Third rung: the same task with three things from the classroom, before the question's own things return.

writeup.delight: When the last prefix card turns over on the second phase, the whole row of worths slides into one line under the chart, a thousand times at one end and a thousandth at the other, and the base unit glows once in the middle.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet placed. On the first phase the three standard unit cards, metre, kilogram and litre, stand above the chart with a tray of things below them: a ribbon, a bag of rice, a bucket of water and more. On the second the chart lies with its six prefix cards face down and the base unit column lit. On the third one row of the chart lies with the marker on a unit and ten small bars of the unit to its right beside it. On the fourth a row lies empty with the deep blue digit tiles in their tray and the point loose above. One thing moves, once: the first thing in the tray, the first prefix card, the Step left button or the loose point gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any digits dropped on any row of the chart, the point set after any unit, and the measure read back in that unit. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the standard units, the prefixes, neighbouring units, and a measure read as one decimal with its unit.
voiceLines: A chart of units, waiting to be built.
What would you measure this with? Drop it on its unit.
Turn a card. How many base units is it worth?
Step left. How many of the old unit fill the new one?
Set the point after the unit asked for. Now say the unit too.
A new row of the chart. Build it the same way.
Free play. Drop any digits and set the point anywhere.
Look along the row. Which unit is next to which?
You built the chart and read a measure off it, with its unit.

observations.why: the middle column holds the base unit the prefixes are added to, and the standard unit of weight is the kilogram.
observations.soWhat: keep the two words apart: the kilogram is the standard unit, and the gram is the base unit.
observations.observe: The gram sat in the middle column, but the kilogram card was the one the rice bag went on.

observations.why: kilo, hecto and deca make bigger units, and deci, centi and milli make smaller ones.
observations.soWhat: the prefix alone tells how big a unit is against its base unit.
observations.observe: The prefix cards to the left of the base unit showed times, and the ones to its right showed parts.

observations.why: each unit is 10 times the unit to its right.
observations.soWhat: two steps make a hundred and three steps make a thousand, so the chart shows how far apart any two units are.
observations.observe: Every Step left made ten bars click into one.

observations.why: the point sits just after the digit of the unit named, and each column is one unit.
observations.soWhat: a decimal measure means nothing until its unit is named with it.
observations.observe: The same digits read as a different decimal each time the point moved to another unit.

source_tool.name: Chart Builder
source_tool.blurb: Build the metric chart from kilo to milli around the base unit, see each unit grow ten times to the left, and read a measure written one digit to a unit as one decimal with its unit.

serves.exercise: naming the smallest unit of length, weight and capacity in the chart
filling blanks from the metric chart, including how many times a unit grows or shrinks along it
writing three mixed measures as decimals
making flashcards for nine vocabulary words

source_tool.description: A chart of seven columns fills the working area: kilo, hecto, deca, the base unit, deci, centi and milli, from left to right, with a row each for length, weight and capacity. The middle column holds the base units metre, gram and litre, and the unit names are violet, labelled Unit. Above the chart three standard unit cards, metre, kilogram and litre, wait for things to be dropped on them: a ribbon, a bag of rice, a bucket of water and more. A tap on a prefix card lights its worth against the base unit, 1000 times, 100 times, 10 times, 1/10, 1/100 or 1/1000, as a violet Unit fact. A step button moves the amber marker one column to the left, and ten small bars of the unit to its right slide together to fill one bar of the new unit, the step labelled Move in vermilion. On the last phase deep blue digit tiles, labelled Given, are dropped one to a column, the child sets the point after the digit of the unit they choose, and the measure is read back in green, labelled Answer, as one decimal with that unit's name. A zero that holds an empty column open is grey, labelled Place holder. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of units placed on the chart.
source_tool.art_direction: Labelled cards on a classroom floor / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a unit chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, rulers and tapes marked in their units, kitchen scales, measuring jugs marked in millilitres, and thermometers with labelled marks.
Every measure is written with its unit on every line, and every decimal names the unit it is in, so 3.04 L is never shown as a bare 3.04.
Every mixed measure shown is ordinary: its smaller part is less than one of the larger unit.
Places are counted from the unit the child has to the unit the child wants, one hop at a time, and each hop shows the number, not the unit, divided or multiplied by 10.
Multiplying and dividing a measure happen in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and a sharing that does not come out even shows what is left over.
A thermometer shows what one small mark is worth before its column is read, and a Celsius reading sits beside a Fahrenheit one only in the four pairs the chapter prints.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a hop across the chart, a carry across units, a length shared into equal pieces, or a column rising to a mark.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a unit or a mark the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the measure the question gives is deep blue, and the measure the working reaches, with a reading taken off a scale, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The places moved across the unit chart, each one dividing or multiplying the number by 10, and the worth of one small mark on a scale are vermilion. A unit fact such as 1 kg = 1000 g, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet. The part taken away, and a remainder left over after sharing, are rose. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Move, Unit fact, Taken away, Left over and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look along the row. Which unit is next to which?
voice.onNext: A new row of the chart. Build it the same way.
voice.opening: A chart of units, waiting to be built.
voice.onFinish: You built the chart and read a measure off it, with its unit.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Drop any digits and set the point anywhere.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Ten times the unit to its right

placement.where: After the class has laid the prefix cards out on the floor with the base unit card in the middle, and has said what each card is worth. The tool is what fills one unit with ten of its neighbour and moves the point, which the floor cards cannot.

answer_key.rule: The standard unit of length is the metre, the standard unit of weight is the kilogram, and the standard unit of capacity is the litre. The chart adds a prefix to a base unit, metre, gram or litre: kilo means 1000 times, hecto 100 times, deca 10 times, deci 1/10, centi 1/100 and milli 1/1000. Each unit is 10 times the unit to its right, and 1/10 of the unit to its left. The smallest units in the chart are the millimetre, the milligram and the millilitre. A measure written one digit to a unit is read as one decimal: the point goes just after the digit of the unit you choose, and that unit is named with the decimal.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps what the child placed. A thing on the wrong standard unit stays there, and the unit that measures its kind is lit amber beside it. A point set after the wrong column stays, and the measure is read back in the unit the point sits after, with the unit the question asked for lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A hose has a length, so it is measured in the standard unit of length, the metre.
A pumpkin has a weight, so it is measured in the standard unit of weight, the kilogram.
Water in a tank has a capacity, so it is measured in the standard unit of capacity, the litre.
So the three standard units are the metre, the kilogram and the litre.
items.answer: The metre for the hose, the kilogram for the pumpkin, and the litre for the water.
items.question: Which standard unit measures the length of a garden hose, which measures the weight of a pumpkin, and which measures the water in a tank?
items.checkpoint: The standard units are the metre for length, the kilogram for weight and the litre for capacity.
items.misconception: Choosing the gram for the standard unit of weight, because the gram sits in the middle column. The middle column holds the base unit, and the standard unit of weight is the kilogram.

steps: The prefixes are added to a base unit, and for weight the base unit is the gram.
Kilo means 1000 times, hecto 100 times and deca 10 times.
So a hectogram is 100 times a gram.
items.answer: Hecto means 100 times the base unit, so 100 g make 1 hg.
items.question: What does hecto mean, and how many grams make 1 hg?
items.checkpoint: Each prefix says what the unit is worth against the base unit: hecto means 100 times.
items.misconception: Taking hecto for 1/100, because it sounds like hundredths; the prefixes for hundredths and thousandths are centi and milli.

steps: Each unit is 10 times the unit to its right.
dL sits just to the left of cL, so 1 dL is 10 cL.
The litre sits just to the left of dL, so 1 litre is 10 dL.
Each dL is 10 cL, so 1 litre is 100 cL.
items.answer: 10 cL make 1 dL, and 100 cL make 1 litre.
items.question: On the capacity row, dL sits just to the left of cL. How many centilitres make 1 dL, and how many make 1 litre?
items.checkpoint: Each unit is 10 times the unit to its right, and 1/10 of the unit to its left.
items.misconception: Counting only one step from cL to the litre, when the litre is two steps to the left, and so giving ten times too few centilitres.

steps: Put 3 under kL, 7 under hL, 2 under daL and 5 under L.
The question asks for kilolitres, so the point goes just after the kL digit.
The digits after the point are 7, 2 and 5.
So the tank holds 3.725 kL, which is 3 kL 7 hL 2 daL 5 L, and the unit kL is written with it.
items.question: A tank holds 3 kL 7 hL 2 daL 5 L. Write it on the chart one digit to a unit, and read it as one decimal in kilolitres.
items.checkpoint: The point goes just after the digit of the unit asked for, and that unit is named with the decimal.
items.misconception: Setting the point after the L digit and reading 3725 with no unit named, so nobody can tell what the number measures.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.

learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Which standard unit would you use to measure the length of a playground?
What does deca mean? How many litres make 1 daL?
items.final_answer: Deca means 10 times the base unit, so 10 litres make 1 daL

items.question: Digits 4, 1 and 7 sit under kg, hg and dag, and 0 sits under g. Read the measure as one decimal in kilograms.
Which standard unit fits the water in a bucket, and which fits the weight of a bag of potatoes?
items.final_answer: The litre for the water, and the kilogram for the potatoes

items.question: Which is the largest unit of length in the chart, and how many metres make one of it?
How many places is it from mm to m on the chart, and how many millimetres make 1 m?
items.final_answer: Three places to the left; 1 m is 10 x 10 x 10 = 1000 mm

items.question: Write 7 km 0 hm 3 dam 6 m as one decimal in kilometres.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: drops a thing onto a standard unit card on the first phase
lights what the prefix is worth against the base unit
moves the marker one column left and fills one unit with ten of the unit to its right
drop one digit under each column of a row
is set just after the digit of the unit chosen
types a number, a decimal or a unit name

teaching_notes: Lay the chart out by hand first, with the base unit card in the middle. Keep the page's words: the kilogram is the standard unit of weight, and the gram is the base unit the prefixes are added to. Say each unit is 10 times the unit to its right, never that the units are tens of the standard unit. When the smallest unit is asked for, say the smallest unit in the chart, because smaller metric units exist. Name the unit with every decimal. The nine flashcard words, metre, gram, litre and the six prefixes, are the cards of this chart.
generation_prompt: Build a metric chart tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Seven columns, kilo, hecto, deca, the base unit, deci, centi and milli, in rows for length, weight and capacity, with the unit names in violet and the base unit column in the middle. On the first phase things are dragged onto three standard unit cards, metre, kilogram and litre. Prefix cards turn over to show their worth against the base unit as a violet unit fact. A Step left button moves an amber marker one column left and slides ten small bars of the unit to its right into one bar, labelled Move in vermilion. On the last phase deep blue digit tiles drop one to a column, a point is set after a chosen unit's digit, and the decimal is read back in green with its unit named; a zero holding a column open is grey. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Build the chart. Step left and watch ten of a unit make one. Drop one digit under each unit, set the point after the unit asked for, and say the unit with the decimal.
